questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons that the third energy level (n = 3) can hold?
questions.explanation: Each energy level holds up to 2n² electrons, so n = 3 holds 2 × 3² = 18, in its 3s, 3p and 3d sublevels. Eight is the number of electrons in the outer shell of argon, where the 3d sublevel is still empty.

questions.stem: How many orbitals make up a p sublevel, and how many electrons can it hold?
options: 1 orbital holding up to 2 electrons
5 orbitals holding up to 10 electrons
3 orbitals holding up to 3 electrons
3 orbitals holding up to 6 electrons
questions.explanation: A p sublevel has three orbitals, and each orbital holds at most two electrons, so a p sublevel holds six. One orbital is an s sublevel, and five orbitals is a d sublevel.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of electrons in a single orbital?
options: Eight, as in a full shell
One, in any sublevel
Two, with opposite spins
Two, with the same spin
questions.explanation: Any orbital, whether s, p or d, holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins. Eight electrons fill the s and p sublevels of an outer shell, which together contain four orbitals.

questions.stem: Which list shows these sublevels in order of increasing energy, as they fill in atoms up to krypton?
questions.explanation: The 4s sublevel is lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: potassium and calcium put electrons into 4s before scandium starts filling 3d. The 4p sublevel fills after 3d, from gallium to krypton.

questions.stem: Which statement about the energy of electrons in an atom is correct?
options: In the same shell, a p electron has more energy than an s electron
All electrons in the same shell have exactly the same energy
Electrons nearer the nucleus have more energy than outer ones
An electron in a 1s orbital has the highest energy in the atom
questions.explanation: In atoms with more than one electron, each shell is split into sublevels of different energy, in the order s < p < d. Electrons close to the nucleus are the most strongly held and have the lowest energy.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of a sulfur atom (Z = 16)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁸ 3s² 3p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
questions.explanation: Sixteen electrons fill 1s (2), 2s (2), 2p (6) and 3s (2), leaving four for 3p. 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ has 18 electrons, which is the sulfide ion, and a p sublevel can never hold eight.

questions.stem: What is the electron configuration of an iron atom (Z = 26)?
options: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁸
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p⁶
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁴ 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶
questions.explanation: After argon (18 electrons), the 4s sublevel fills with two electrons and the remaining six go into 3d. The 4p sublevel only starts to fill once 3d is full, at gallium.

questions.stem: Using [Ar] to stand for 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, what is the electron configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Fe, Z = 26)?
options: [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶
[Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵
[Ar] 3d⁶
[Ar] 4s² 3d⁴
questions.explanation: When transition metals form ions, the 4s electrons are lost before the 3d electrons. The iron atom is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, so removing the two 4s electrons gives [Ar] 3d⁶. Removing 3d electrons first is a common error.

questions.stem: Copper (Z = 29) is an exception to the usual filling order. Using [Ar] for 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶, what is its ground-state configuration?
options: [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s²
[Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4p¹
[Ar] 3d⁸ 4s² 4p¹
[Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹
questions.explanation: Copper has a full 3d sublevel and a single 4s electron, an arrangement more stable than the predicted [Ar] 3d⁹ 4s². Chromium is the other exception up to krypton, with [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s¹.

questions.stem: Which ion has the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶?
options: Ca²⁺
Cl⁻
K⁺
Mg²⁺
questions.explanation: A magnesium atom (Z = 12) loses its two 3s electrons to leave 10 electrons, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. Ca²⁺, Cl⁻ and K⁺ each have 18 electrons, the configuration of argon.

questions.stem: A particle has atomic number 16 and the electron configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. What is its charge?
questions.explanation: Atomic number 16 means 16 protons, but the configuration shows 18 electrons. Two more electrons than protons gives a charge of 2−, the sulfide ion.

questions.stem: Which ion does calcium (Z = 20) form, and what is its electron configuration?
options: Ca⁺, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹
Ca²⁺, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
Ca²⁻, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
Ca²⁺, 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴
questions.explanation: Calcium is in group 2 and loses its two 4s electrons to reach the stable configuration of argon. The configuration ending in 3p⁴ has only 16 electrons, two fewer than Ca²⁺ has, and calcium never gains electrons to form a negative ion.

questions.stem: An element has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p⁵. Where is it in the periodic table?
options: Period 4, group 15, p-block
Period 4, group 17, p-block
Period 5, group 17, p-block
Period 4, group 7, d-block
questions.explanation: The highest occupied shell is n = 4, so it is in period 4. The last electron enters a 4p sublevel, putting it in the p-block, and seven outer electrons (4s² 4p⁵) place it in group 17. The element is bromine.

questions.stem: The elements from scandium to zinc belong to which block of the periodic table?
options: The d-block
The s-block
The p-block
The f-block
questions.explanation: From scandium to zinc, electrons are being added to the 3d sublevel, so these transition metals form the d-block. Groups 1 and 2 form the s-block and groups 13 to 18 the p-block.

questions.stem: Magnesium and calcium are both in group 2. What do their atoms have in common?
options: Two electrons in each p sublevel
Two electrons in their outer s sublevel
Two occupied main energy levels
The same number of neutrons
questions.explanation: Group 2 elements all end in ns², two outer s electrons, which is why they have similar chemistry and form 2+ ions. The number of occupied energy levels sets the period, not the group.

questions.stem: An element is in period 3 of the periodic table. What does this tell you about its atoms?
options: They have three electrons in their outer shell
They have three electrons in a p sublevel
They form ions with a charge of 3+ or 3−
Their electrons occupy three main energy levels
questions.explanation: The period number equals the number of occupied main energy levels, so every period 3 atom has electrons in the first, second and third shells. The number of outer-shell electrons is given by the group.

questions.stem: What colour does a sodium compound give in a flame test?
options: Lilac
Blue-green
Apple green
Yellow-orange
questions.explanation: Sodium gives an intense yellow-orange flame. Potassium gives lilac, copper(II) blue-green and barium a pale apple green.

questions.stem: A solution gives a blue-green flame in a flame test. Which metal ion is it most likely to contain?
options: Cu²⁺
Na⁺
K⁺
Ca²⁺
questions.explanation: Copper(II) ions give a characteristic blue-green flame. Sodium gives yellow-orange, potassium lilac and calcium orange-red.

questions.stem: Why does a metal salt give a coloured flame when it is heated?
options: Electrons absorb light from the flame and reflect back only one colour of it
Electrons gain energy, jump to higher levels, then emit light as they drop back
Electrons are lost from the atoms, and the ions left behind glow as they cool
The metal reacts with oxygen in the flame and gives out its chemical energy as light
questions.explanation: Heat excites electrons to higher energy levels. As each falls back to a lower level it emits a photon whose energy equals the energy gap, and these photons give the flame its colour.

questions.stem: Barium gives a green flame and strontium a red flame. Which statement explains the difference?
options: The main transitions in barium release more energy per photon than those in strontium
Barium atoms have more electrons, so they emit more photons than strontium atoms
Barium ions are larger, so their electrons fall further and emit lower-energy light
Strontium absorbs green light from the flame, so only its red light is left behind
questions.explanation: Green light has a shorter wavelength and higher photon energy than red light. The colour depends on the size of the energy gaps electrons fall across, which differ for each element, not on the number of photons.

questions.stem: How is a flame test related to atomic emission spectroscopy?
options: A flame test uses ions in solution, while a spectrum needs atoms in the solid
A flame test shows a continuous rainbow, while a spectrum shows a single colour
A flame shows the mixed colour of all emitted light; a spectrum splits it into lines
A flame test measures absorbed light, while a spectrum measures emitted light
questions.explanation: Both rely on light emitted by excited electrons. The eye sees the blend of every wavelength as one colour, while a spectroscope separates it into a pattern of lines that identifies the element.

questions.stem: Why does the emission spectrum of an element consist of separate coloured lines rather than a continuous band?
options: Atoms only emit light when they collide, which happens at regular intervals
Electrons can only occupy fixed energy levels, so only certain energy gaps exist
The element emits every colour, but most of them are absorbed by the flame gases
Each line comes from a different isotope of the element present in the sample
questions.explanation: Electron energy levels are discrete, so an electron falling from one level to another emits a photon of one particular energy and wavelength. Each possible transition gives one line.

questions.stem: A solid contains both sodium and potassium salts. Why is emission spectroscopy more useful than a flame test for identifying the metals?
options: A spectroscope heats the sample hotter, so both metals react with the oxygen
Emission spectroscopy measures the mass of each ion as well as its colour
A flame test only works on pure metals, not on compounds such as salts
Each element's lines can be picked out, even when one flame colour masks another
questions.explanation: Sodium's intense yellow flame hides the faint lilac of potassium. A spectroscope separates the light into each element's characteristic lines, so both can be identified in the mixture.

questions.stem: Which is a use of atomic emission spectroscopy in industry or medicine?
options: Identifying the functional groups present in an organic molecule
Finding the molar mass of an unknown gas from its density
Determining the shape of a protein from its crystal structure
Checking the metal composition of an alloy during steel making
questions.explanation: Atomic emission spectroscopy identifies and measures metal elements from the light their excited atoms emit, so it can check the elements in an alloy or the sodium and potassium in a blood sample. Functional groups are found by infrared spectroscopy.

questions.stem: Which lists these period 3 elements in order of decreasing atomic radius?
options: Mg > Na > Cl > Si
Na > Cl > Mg > Si
Na > Mg > Si > Cl
Cl > Si > Mg > Na
questions.explanation: Across a period, the nuclear charge increases while electrons are added to the same shell, so the outer electrons are pulled closer. Atomic radius therefore decreases from sodium to chlorine.

questions.stem: Why does atomic radius increase down group 1 from lithium to potassium?
options: The electrons repel the nucleus more strongly as the group is descended
Each element has one more occupied electron shell than the one above
The nuclear charge decreases down the group, so electrons are held less
Each element has one more electron in its outer shell than the one above
questions.explanation: Down a group, each element adds a new shell further from the nucleus, and the inner shells shield the outer electron. Nuclear charge actually increases down the group, and every group 1 atom has one outer electron.

questions.stem: Why is a sodium ion, Na⁺, smaller than a sodium atom?
options: It has gained an electron, which is shared with the nucleus more closely
It has lost its only 3s electron, so it has one fewer occupied shell
It has gained a proton, which pulls the electrons closer to the nucleus
It has lost a neutron, which makes the nucleus and the ion smaller
questions.explanation: Sodium (2,8,1) loses its single outer electron to become Na⁺ (2,8). With the third shell empty, the outermost electrons are in the second shell, much closer to the nucleus. The number of protons does not change.

questions.stem: Why is a chloride ion, Cl⁻, larger than a chlorine atom?
options: The added electron goes into a new fourth shell further from the nucleus
The chloride ion has fewer protons, so the electrons are attracted less strongly
The chloride ion has lost an electron, which reduces the attraction to the nucleus
The added electron increases electron repulsion while the nuclear charge is unchanged
questions.explanation: Gaining an electron puts 18 electrons around the same 17 protons. The extra repulsion between electrons spreads them out, so the ion is larger. The electron enters the 3p sublevel, not a new shell.

questions.stem: The ions O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺ and Mg²⁺ all have 10 electrons. Which lists them in order of decreasing radius?
options: Na⁺ > Mg²⁺ > O²⁻ > F⁻
F⁻ > O²⁻ > Mg²⁺ > Na⁺
O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺
Mg²⁺ > Na⁺ > F⁻ > O²⁻
questions.explanation: With the same number of electrons, the radius depends on nuclear charge: oxygen has 8 protons and magnesium 12. The more protons pulling on the same 10 electrons, the smaller the ion, so O²⁻ is the largest and Mg²⁺ the smallest.

questions.stem: What is the first ionisation energy of an element?
options: The energy to remove all the electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms
The energy to break one mole of bonds between atoms of the element
The energy to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms
The energy released when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain one electron
questions.explanation: First ionisation energy refers to removing the most loosely held electron from each atom in a mole of gaseous atoms, forming 1+ ions. The energy change when atoms gain an electron is a different quantity.

questions.stem: Why does first ionisation energy generally increase across period 3?
options: The atoms become larger across the period, so electrons are harder to reach
Nuclear charge rises while electrons enter the same shell, so they are held more tightly
Each element has one more shell, so its outer electrons are further from the nucleus
Shielding by the inner electrons increases sharply across the period
questions.explanation: Across a period, protons are added but the outer electrons stay in the same shell with similar shielding, so they feel a stronger attraction and are harder to remove. Atoms get smaller, not larger, across a period.

questions.stem: First ionisation energies are Na 496, Mg 738 and Al 578 kJ mol⁻¹. Why is the value for aluminium lower than for magnesium?
options: Aluminium is a metalloid, so it holds on to its outer electrons less strongly
Aluminium's outer electron is in the 3p sublevel, which is higher in energy than 3s
Aluminium has fewer protons than magnesium, so it holds its electrons less tightly
Aluminium's outer electron is in a fourth shell, further from the nucleus than 3s
questions.explanation: Magnesium's outer electrons are in 3s, but aluminium's highest-energy electron is alone in 3p, which is higher in energy and slightly more shielded, so it is easier to remove. This breaks the general rise across the period.

questions.stem: Why is the first ionisation energy of potassium lower than that of sodium?
options: Potassium has fewer protons, so it attracts its outer electron less
Potassium's outer electron is in a p sublevel rather than an s sublevel
Potassium has more electrons in its outer shell than sodium does
Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded
questions.explanation: Potassium's outer electron is in the fourth shell, further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner electrons, so it is easier to remove. Potassium has more protons (19) than sodium (11), but the extra shielding outweighs them.

questions.stem: What does the electronegativity of an element measure?
options: The ability of its atoms to attract the shared electrons in a covalent bond
The energy needed to remove the outer electron from one of its atoms
The number of electrons its atoms gain when they form a negative ion
The negative charge carried by its ions in an ionic compound
questions.explanation: Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom pulls on the electron pair it shares in a bond. Ionisation energy, the energy to remove an electron, is a related but different property.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the trend in electronegativity in the periodic table?
options: It decreases across a period and increases down a group
It increases across a period and increases down a group
It decreases across a period and decreases down a group
It increases across a period and decreases down a group
questions.explanation: Electronegativity rises across a period as nuclear charge increases and atomic radius falls, and it falls down a group as the bonding electrons are further from the nucleus. Fluorine is the most electronegative element.

questions.stem: Element X is in period 3, group 2, and element Y is in period 3, group 16. Which comparison is correct?
options: X has a smaller atomic radius and lower electronegativity than Y
X has a larger atomic radius and lower first ionisation energy than Y
X has a smaller atomic radius and higher first ionisation energy than Y
X has a larger atomic radius and higher electronegativity than Y
questions.explanation: X (magnesium) is to the left of Y (sulfur) in the same period, so it has a lower nuclear charge holding the same shells. It is larger, gives up electrons more easily and is less electronegative.

questions.stem: Rubidium is directly below potassium in group 1. Compared with potassium, rubidium is predicted to have:
options: a larger atomic radius, lower first ionisation energy and lower electronegativity
a larger atomic radius, higher first ionisation energy and lower electronegativity
a smaller atomic radius, lower first ionisation energy and higher electronegativity
a larger atomic radius, lower first ionisation energy and higher electronegativity
questions.explanation: Rubidium has one more occupied shell than potassium, so its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded. It is larger, loses its outer electron more easily and attracts bonding electrons less strongly.
